# Introduction to Jeremiah

## Part 1: General Introduction

### Outline of the Book of Jeremiah

1. Yahweh calls Jeremiah to be a prophet (1:1–19))
2. Yahweh will judge and punish Judah (2:1–29:32)
    * Judah called to repent of spiritual adultery (2:1–6:30)
    * Judah judged for its false religion (7:1–10:16)
    * Jeremiah stands between Yahweh and his people (11:1–20:19)
    * Jeremiah confronts his people (21:1–29:32)
3. Yahweh promises to restore Judah (30:1–33:26)
    * Yahweh will bring the people of Judah back to their land (30:1–24)
    * Yahweh will create a new covenant with them (31:1–40)
    * The people will come back (32:1–44)
    * Kings descended from David will rule again (33:1–26)
4. Jeremiah suffers (34:1–45:5)
    * Before Yahweh punishes Judah (34:1–36:32)
    * While Yahweh punishes Judah (37:1–39:18)
    * After Yahweh punishes Judah (40:1–45:5)
5. Yahweh will judge and punish the nations (46:1–51:64)
    * Egypt (46:1–28)
    * Philistia (47:1–28)
    * Moab (48:1–47)
    * Ammon (49:1–6)
    * Edom (49:7–22)
    * Damascus (49:23–27)
    * Kedar (49:28–33)
    * Elam (49:34–39)
    * Babylonia (50:1–51:64)
6. Jerusalem captured and destroyed (52:1–34)

### What is the Book of Jeremiah about?

The Book of Jeremiah gives the prophesies of a priest named Jeremiah. It also tells how Jeremiah suffered in different ways while he prophesied.

Jeremiah began prophesying about 626 B.C. After the death of King Josiah, many groups of people in Israel opposed Jeremiah. Some of these people wanted to depend on Egypt to protect the nation. Others were idol worshipers. They hated Jeremiah for denouncing their gods.

During the reign of King Jehoiakim, Jeremiah prophesied about the temple of Yahweh. King Jehoiakim received some of these prophecies in writing and burned the document. The next king, Zedekiah, put Jeremiah in prison when he told the king to surrender to Babylon.

King Nebuchadnezzar of Babylonia invaded Judah in 597 B.C. He conquered Jerusalem in 587 B.C. He offered Jeremiah housing and money if Jeremiah would go to Babylon. But Jeremiah remained in Jerusalem to help the few Jews left there.

Shortly after that, Gedaliah, whom Nebuchadnezzar had chosen to be governor over Judah, was murdered. Some Jewish rebels captured Jeremiah and took him to Egypt. Those rebels went to Egypt to be protected there rather than to live under Nebuchadnezzar’s rule. Jeremiah may have died soon after being taken to Egypt. But while in Egypt he prophesied that the Babylonians would invade and conquer Egypt.

### How should the title of this book be translated?

The traditional title of this book is “The Book of Jeremiah” or just “Jeremiah.” Translators may also call it the “The Book about Jeremiah” or “What the Prophet Jeremiah Said.”

### Who wrote the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah was a priest and a prophet living in Judah. He spoke the prophesies in the Book of Jeremiah. A friend named Baruch wrote down many of the prophecies as Jeremiah spoke them to him.

## Part 2: Important Religious and Cultural Concepts

### What is the new covenant that is presented in the Book of Jeremiah?

Jeremiah introduced a “new covenant” between Yahweh and Israel (chapter 31). Yahweh would “write this covenant on the hearts” of the people. This means that the covenant would be a part of the people instead of just written on stone or paper. The people would obey the new covenant with all their heart.

### What relationship do Jeremiah’s prophecies have to the other nations besides Israel?

Much of the Old Testament before this time is only about the nation of Israel. But Jeremiah also spoke of how Yahweh would judge other nations of the world. Yahweh would also punish the other nations for their wicked deeds.

## Part 3: Important Translation Issues

### Are the events in the Book of Jeremiah told in the order that they actually happened?

Many of the events in the Book of Jeremiah are not told in the order that they actually happened. Instead, the various prophecies appear to be arranged by topic.

### Why does the Book of Jeremiah refer to this prophet as “he” or “him”?

Many times in the book, the author refers to Jeremiah as “Jeremiah” or “he.” This is unusual if Jeremiah wrote the book. The reason this occurs is perhaps because Baruch, Jeremiah’s secretary, wrote down some parts of the book. Translators should keep the words “Jeremiah” and “he.”

# Jeremiah 1 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from a dated heading (1:1–3) to Jeremiah’s call (1:4–10), two visions (1:11–16), and Yahweh’s charge (1:17–19). The ULT formats 1:5 and 1:7–8 as poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Commissioning a prophet

Yahweh set Jeremiah apart before birth and put his words in Jeremiah’s mouth. (See: [prophet](tw:prophet))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Wordplay in 1:11–12

The Hebrew word for “almond” sounds like the word for “watching,” which is the point of Yahweh’s reply.
2:
# Jeremiah 2 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This is a covenant lawsuit in poetry. Yahweh recalls Israel’s early devotion (2:1–3), indicts the nation for abandoning him (2:4–19), and exposes its unfaithfulness (2:20–37).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Israel as an unfaithful wife

Yahweh pictures the covenant as a marriage, so idolatry appears as prostitution. (See: [prostitute](tw:prostitute))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Rhetorical questions

Yahweh accuses mainly through rhetorical questions, and paired lines often restate one idea.
3:
# Jeremiah 3 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Poetry and prose alternate: there is an appeal to unfaithful Judah (3:1–5), a contrast of apostate Israel and treacherous Judah (3:6–11), a call to return (3:12–18), and a closing confession (3:19–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The law about divorce

Verse 1 assumes the existence of the law forbidding a remarried woman to return to her first husband (see Deuteronomy 24:1-4). Yahweh applies it to Israel and Judah as adulterous wives. (See: [adultery](tw:adultery))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting speakers

Yahweh, the prophet, and the people all speak, and the changes are unmarked.
4:
# Jeremiah 4 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from a call for Israel to return to Yahweh (4:1–4) to poetic alarm over an invading army from the north (4:5–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

In 4:4, circumcision, the covenant sign, is an image of inward devotion. (See: [circumcise](tw:circumcise))

### Jeremiah’s accusation that Yahweh deceived the people

In 4:10, Jeremiah says to Yahweh, “Ah, Lord Yahweh, surely deceiving, you have deceived this people and Jerusalem, saying, ‘It will be peace for you.’ Yet the sword will reach as far as the life.” Here Jeremiah is not stating the Yahweh himself promised the people of Judah “peace.” Rather, he is saying that it was the false prophets who deceived the people. Jeremiah is expressing his frustration that the people of Judah are about to be slaughtered. He knows Yahweh is sovereign and could have stopped this from happening, so he is expressing his complaint to Yahweh because he knows that Yahweh is ultimately responsible for allowing the people of Judah to be deceived by the deceptive messages of the false prophets.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The speaker shifts without announcement among Yahweh, Jeremiah, and the people, so you may need to identify each speaker.
5:
# Jeremiah 5 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry about a search through Jerusalem for one just person (5:1–9), a warning of an invading nation (5:10–19), and an indictment of a people who will not fear Yahweh (5:20–31).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Lying prophets

The prophets speak falsely, the priests rule by their own authority, and the people approve. (See: [prophet](tw:prophet))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

Speakers change without announcement, and the people’s words are quoted inside Yahweh’s speech.
6:
# Jeremiah 6 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter comprised poetry throughout: alarm to flee the army from the north (6:1–8), Yahweh’s verdict on people who will not listen (6:9–21), terror as the army advances (6:22–26), and Jeremiah as a tester of metal (6:27–30).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Uncircumcised ear

In 6:10, the covenant sign becomes an image for ears that will not hear Yahweh. (See: [circumcise](tw:circumcise))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

Yahweh, Jeremiah, the attackers, and the people speak without announcement, at times quoted inside another speaker’s words.
7:
# Jeremiah 7 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh commands Jeremiah to preach at the gate of the temple, calling Judah to amend its conduct and warning that the sanctuary will not protect Judah.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Trust in the temple

The people of Judah assumed the temple guaranteed their safety; Yahweh cites the Tabernacle at Shiloh as a sanctuary of Yahweh that he destroyed because of the Israelites persistent breaking of his covenant.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Listening as obeying or paying attention

In this chapter the word “listen” means “pay attention” or “obey” every time it occurs. If possible, translate this word consistently so that readers can see the reoccurring theme.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s speech contains up to three nested levels of quoted speech, and “the declaration of Yahweh” interrupts it mid-sentence.
8:
# Jeremiah 8 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues Yahweh’s judgment speech from chapter 7, moving from desecrated graves (verses 1–3), to the refusal to repent (verses 4–13), to invasion and lament (verses 14–22).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The host of the heavens

The people worshiped the sun, moon, and stars as gods. (See: [falsegod](tw:falsegod))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked speaker changes

The speaker shifts among Yahweh, the people, and the prophet without introduction, notably at verses 14, 18, and 19.
9:
# Jeremiah 9 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is mostly poetry, moving from Jeremiah’s lament over his people’s deceit to Yahweh’s sentence of refining, desolation, and exile.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Circumcision of the heart

Verses 25–26 contrast bodily circumcision with the inward loyalty to Yahweh that Israel lacks.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The speaker shifts between Jeremiah and Yahweh without introduction, and verses 15, 19, and 22 nest quotations within quotations.
10:
# Jeremiah 10 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter contrasts the worthless idols of the nations with Yahweh, the living God and creator (verses 1–16), then announces the coming exile and Jeremiah’s lament (verses 17–25).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Making idols

Verses 3–5, 9, and 14 describe craftsmen shaping false gods from wood and overlaying them with silver and gold.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The chapter shifts speakers without warning between Yahweh, Jeremiah, and the personified city.
11:
# Jeremiah 11 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to proclaim the covenant and its curses to Judah (verses 1-17); Jeremiah then laments a plot against his life (verses 18-23).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Covenant curses

Judah broke the covenant Yahweh made at the exodus and built altars to Baal, so its curses now fall as disaster.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Listening as obeying or paying attenting

In this chapter the word “listen” means “pay attention” or “obey” every time it is used of people listening to Yahweh and each time it speaks of Yahweh listening to people it means “to pay attention.” If possible, translate this word consistently so that readers can see the reoccurring theme.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s messages nest speech several layers deep. Consider marking the levels clearly or making inner quotations indirect.
12:
# Jeremiah 12 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Verses 1-13 are poetry. Jeremiah complains that wicked people prosper (verses 1-4); Yahweh answers (verses 5-6), laments abandoning his people (verses 7-13), and promises to uproot and restore Judah’s neighbors (verses 14-17).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Yahweh’s inheritance

Yahweh calls his people his house, his inheritance, and his vineyard.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked speaker changes

The speaker shifts between Jeremiah and Yahweh without introduction.
13:
# Jeremiah 13 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Prose sign acts—the ruined linen loincloth (verses 1–11) and the wine jars (verses 12–14)—give way to poetry announcing exile for Judah’s pride (verses 15–27).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Prophetic sign acts

Yahweh had Jeremiah perform symbolic actions and then explained them as pictures of Judah’s ruin and coming exile.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Verses 12–14 nest quotations several levels deep; some languages may need indirect speech.
14:
# Jeremiah 14 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh, Jeremiah, and the people speak in turn about a drought, false prophets, and judgment. Verses 7-9 and 19-22 are communal laments.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Drought as judgment

Withheld rain signaled judgment on covenant unfaithfulness; the dry wells of verses 2-6 mark Judah’s guilt.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked speaker changes

The speaker changes without introduction at verses 7, 13, and 19, so translators may need to name each speaker.
15:
# Jeremiah 15 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter moves from Yahweh’s refusal to spare Judah (verses 1–9) to Jeremiah’s lament and Yahweh’s answer to him (verses 10–21). Much of it is poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Intercession

Moses and Samuel were remembered as men whose prayers turned Yahweh’s anger aside. Not even their intercession would spare Judah.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of Speaker

The speaker shifts from Yahweh to Jeremiah without introduction at verses 10 and 15.
16:
# Jeremiah 16 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh forbids Jeremiah to marry, to mourn, or to feast, so his life becomes a sign of coming judgment (verses 1–9); verses 10–21 explain the exile and promise a return.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Mourning customs

Verses 5–8 mention the funeral banquet house, ritual gashing and shaving, and the cup of consolation.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s speech often contains further quotations, and the speaker changes to Jeremiah at verse 19.
17:
# Jeremiah 17 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter gathers several short, poetic units that contrast trust in Yahweh with trust in human strength, and it closes with a prose sermon about the Sabbath.

  1. Judah’s engraved sin and the loss of her inheritance (1–4)
  2. Two contrasting portraits of trust (5–8)
    1. Cursed is the man who trusts in mankind, like a shrub in the desert (5–6)
    2. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, like a tree planted by waters (7–8)
  3. The deceitful heart and Yahweh who searches it (9–11)
  4. Jeremiah’s prayer for healing and for vindication against those who mock him (12–18)
  5. Yahweh’s message about the Sabbath at the gates of Jerusalem (19–27)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in (17:1–18).

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Altars, Asherim, and high places

In verses 2–3 the people worship at altars and Asherah poles beside green trees on the hills rather than at the temple. Yahweh treats this worship as the reason he will hand over Judah’s wealth and the land he gave her.

### Keeping the Sabbath holy

In verses 19–27 the command not to bear a burden on the Sabbath refers to carrying goods for trade or doing ordinary work on that day. Yahweh sets obedience and disobedience before the people as two paths with opposite outcomes.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker

The chapter moves between Yahweh speaking, the prophet speaking about the righteous and the wicked, and Jeremiah praying, often with no statement identifying the new speaker. You may need to make each change of speaker explicit.

### Extended comparisons

The contrast in verses 5–8 is developed through two sustained images, a shrub in a salt desert and a tree planted beside water, with a further comparison in verse 11. If your readers would not understand these images, it may help to state the point of each comparison alongside it.
18:
# Jeremiah 18 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to watch a potter at work and then explains what that scene means for Israel, for any nation, and for Judah in particular. The chapter ends with a plot against Jeremiah and his prayer against the men who made it.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the potter’s house (1–4)
  2. Yahweh explains the potter’s work (5–10)
    1. Israel is clay in Yahweh’s hand (5–6)
    2. What Yahweh does to a nation depends on how that nation responds (7–10)
  3. Yahweh calls Judah to turn back, and the people refuse (11–12)
  4. Yahweh accuses Judah of forgetting him and announces that he will scatter them (13–17)
  5. Jeremiah’s opponents plot against him, and he prays against them (18–23)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 18:14–17 and 18/19.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The potter’s house

A potter shaped vessels from clay on a pair of stone wheels that he turned by hand or foot. While the clay was still soft, he could press a spoiled vessel back into a lump and form it into something else. Yahweh uses this everyday scene as a picture of his freedom to deal with his people as he chooses.

### Yahweh relenting from what he has announced

In verses 7–10 Yahweh states that what he announces about a nation is not fixed. If a nation turns from its evil, he will not bring the disaster he spoke of; if a nation does evil, he will not bring the good he promised. This is the basis for his appeal to Judah in verse 11.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

In verse 11 Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to say to the people, and inside that instruction stands a message that begins “Thus says Yahweh” and continues in Yahweh’s own words, stacking three levels of quotation. If this would be confusing in your language, you may translate one or more levels as an indirect quotation.

### A prayer asking for harm to come on enemies

In verses 19–23 Jeremiah asks Yahweh to bring famine, sword, and bereavement on the men who plotted against him and not to forgive their sin. Translate these as requests that Jeremiah addresses to Yahweh, not as predictions of what will happen.

# Jeremiah 19 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

Yahweh sends Jeremiah to buy a clay jar, carry it out to the valley where people have been sacrificing their children, and announce disaster there. Jeremiah then smashes the jar as a picture of what Yahweh will do to Jerusalem, and he repeats the message in the temple courtyard.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah, with a jar, to the Valley of the Son of Hinnom (1–2)
  2. The message Jeremiah proclaims in the valley (3–9)
    1. Why Yahweh is bringing disaster on this place (3–5)
    2. The place will be renamed, and the people will be destroyed (6–9)
  3. Jeremiah breaks the jar and explains what it means (10–13)
  4. Jeremiah repeats the message in the courtyard of the temple (14–15)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Topheth and the Valley of the Son of Hinnom

This valley lay just outside Jerusalem, and Topheth was the site in it where the people burned their sons as offerings to Baal at the worship places they had built there. Yahweh announces that the valley will be renamed “the Valley of Slaughter,” since it will become the place where the people themselves are killed and buried.

### The host of the heavens

Verse 13 refers to worship of the sun, moon, and stars, which the people carried out on the flat roofs of their houses by burning incense and pouring out drink offerings to gods other than Yahweh.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The broken jar as a sign

Jeremiah does not only speak this message; he acts it out by smashing a jar that cannot be mended (verses 10–11). Translate this as something Jeremiah actually does, and keep the connection clear between the smashed jar and what Yahweh says he will do to the people and the city.

### Quotations within quotations

In verses 3–9 and again in verses 11–13, Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to say, Jeremiah is to address his hearers, and a messenger formula such as “Thus says Yahweh of Armies” introduces Yahweh’s own words, so that as many as four levels of quotation stand one inside another. If this would be confusing in your language, you may translate one or more levels as an indirect quotation.

# Jeremiah 20 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter moves from a narrative account of Jeremiah’s public humiliation into a personal lament in which the prophet complains to Yahweh about the cost of his calling.

  1. Pashhur beats Jeremiah and puts him in the stocks (1–2)
  2. Jeremiah renames Pashhur and announces judgment (3–6)
    1. The new name is Magor-Missabib (3)
    2. Yahweh’s message of exile for Pashhur and Judah (4–6)
  3. Jeremiah complains to Yahweh and then praises him (7–13)
    1. The complaint: compelled to speak, mocked by everyone (7–10)
    2. Confidence in Yahweh and a call to praise (11–13)
  4. Jeremiah curses the day of his birth (14–18)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 20:7–18.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Names that announce a fate

When Jeremiah tells Pashhur that Yahweh has renamed him Magor-Missabib, meaning “Terror on Every Side,” he is not merely insulting him. In this culture a name given by God declared what a person would become, so the new name itself announced the judgment described in 20:4–6. Jeremiah’s enemies use the same phrase against him in 20:10.

### The prophet’s lament

The poetry in this chapter belongs to a series of passages in which Jeremiah pours out his distress to Yahweh. Laments like this were an accepted way of speaking to God, so it is best not to soften the prophet’s harsh words into polite complaint.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Unmarked changes of speaker

The chapter changes speakers without introducing them. In 20:3 Jeremiah begins to address Pashhur, in 20:4 he quotes Yahweh inside those words, and in 20:7 he turns abruptly to address Yahweh with no narrative introduction at all. In 20:10 he quotes what his enemies say about him. If this would confuse your readers, you may need to identify each speaker explicitly.

### Praise followed by cursing

In 20:13 Jeremiah calls on others to praise Yahweh for rescuing the needy, and in the very next verse he curses the day he was born. It is best to represent this reversal as it stands rather than smoothing it out, since it expresses the unresolved anguish of the prophet’s situation.
21:
# Jeremiah 21 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins a section of the book that addresses the kings of Judah directly. King Zedekiah asks for a word of rescue, and Yahweh answers that he himself will fight against his own city.

  1. Zedekiah sends messengers to ask Jeremiah to inquire of Yahweh (1–2)
  2. Yahweh answers that he will fight against Jerusalem (3–7)
    1. Yahweh turns the city’s own weapons back against it (3–6)
    2. Zedekiah and the survivors are handed over to Nebuchadnezzar (7)
  3. A message for the people: the way of life and the way of death (8–10)
  4. A message for the royal house of Judah (11–14)
    1. A command to do justice before it is too late (11–12)
    2. An oracle against the city that believes it cannot be attacked (13–14)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 21:12–14.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Inquiring of Yahweh through a prophet

When a crisis came, a king would send officials to a prophet to ask Yahweh what would happen and to request his help. Zedekiah hopes for the kind of miraculous rescue Yahweh had performed in the past, but Yahweh answers that he is the one attacking the city.

### Yahweh fighting against his own people

The words “outstretched hand” and “strong arm” in 21:5 describe the power by which Yahweh rescued Israel from Egypt. Here he turns that same power against Jerusalem, so the language of rescue becomes the language of judgment.

### The duty of the house of David

The kings descended from David were responsible to judge cases fairly and to protect people from those who robbed and oppressed them, and the command in 21:12 holds out the possibility that doing so would turn away Yahweh’s anger.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

From 21:3 onward, several layers of speech are nested inside one another: Jeremiah tells the messengers what to say to Zedekiah, within that he quotes Yahweh, and in 21:13 Yahweh quotes the boast of the city’s inhabitants. If nested quotations would confuse your readers, you may translate some of the inner layers as indirect quotations.

### Changes in the person addressed

The word “you” refers to different people at different points in this chapter, and English does not show the difference. It refers to the two messengers in 21:3, to Zedekiah and his soldiers in 21:4–5, to Jeremiah alone in 21:08, and to the city itself, addressed as a single woman, in 21:13.
22:
# Jeremiah 22 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the section of the book that addresses the kings of Judah. Yahweh sets out what he requires of the royal house, and then pronounces judgment on three kings in turn: Shallum, Jehoiakim, and Coniah.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the royal palace with a call to do justice (1–9)
    1. The command to do justice, and the two outcomes that depend on it (1–5)
    2. An oracle that the palace will become an uninhabited wilderness (6–7)
    3. The nations passing by ask why Yahweh destroyed the city (8–9)
  2. A word about Shallum, who will never return from exile (10–12)
  3. A woe against Jehoiakim, who built his palace by injustice (13–19)
  4. A call to Jerusalem to cry out, because her allies are broken (20–23)
  5. A word about Coniah, the signet ring that Yahweh tears off (24–30)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 22:6–7, 22:13–14, 22:18–23, and 22:28–30.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The king’s duty to do justice

The kings descended from David were responsible to decide cases fairly, to rescue people from those who robbed them, and to protect the sojourner, the fatherless, and the widow, who had no family to defend them. In this chapter Josiah is held up as the king who did this, while his sons are condemned for instead building fine cedar palaces with forced labor .

### Mourning and burial

When someone important died, family and mourners would wail set cries such as “Woe, my brother!” and would bury the body with honor. To say that no one would mourn for Jehoiakim and that he would be buried “with the burial of a donkey,” that is, dragged out and thrown away unburied, describes the most shameful end a person could suffer.

### The signet ring

A signet was a ring or seal that a ruler used to stamp documents, and it stood for his authority. Because a ruler kept it close at hand and would not part with it, Yahweh’s tearing Coniah off “from my right hand” pictures the deliberate removal of a king whom Yahweh had once authorized.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Kings known by more than one name

Shallum in (22:11) is the king called Jehoahaz elsewhere, and Coniah in 22:24 is the king called Jehoiachin and Jeconiah elsewhere. If your readers would be confused by the different names, you could use the more familiar name in your translation or indicate the identification in a footnote.

### Quotations within quotations

In 22:1–5 several layers of speech are nested inside one another: Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to do; within that, Jeremiah is to address the king, and within that, he quotes Yahweh again. The same happens in 22:8–9, where the nations speak to one another. If nested quotations would confuse your readers, you could translate the inner quotations as indirect quotations.

### Changes of speaker and addressee

Yahweh and the prophet speak in turn without being named, and the person addressed shifts as well, from the king to the whole people, to the city of Jerusalem addressed as a woman in 22:20–23, to the land itself in 22:29. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state at each shift who is speaking and who is being addressed.
23:
# Jeremiah 23 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter collects Yahweh’s words against the leaders of Judah—first against the kings, whom he pictures as shepherds, and then, from verse 9 onward, against the prophets who speak in his name although he has not sent them.

  1. Woe to the shepherds, and the promise of a righteous king (1–8)
    1. The shepherds have scattered the flock, and Yahweh will gather it again (1–4)
    2. Yahweh will raise up a righteous branch for David (5–6)
    3. A new rescue will surpass the rescue from Egypt (7–8)
  2. Jeremiah grieves over the corrupt prophets and priests (9–15)
    1. Jeremiah’s anguish and the polluted land (9–12)
    2. The prophets of Samaria and the prophets of Jerusalem (13–15)
  3. Yahweh warns the people not to listen to these prophets (16–24)
    1. They promise peace that Yahweh has not spoken (16–17)
    2. None of them has stood in Yahweh’s counsel (18–22)
    3. No one can hide from the God who fills the heavens and the earth (23–24)
  4. Dreams cannot be compared with the word of Yahweh (25–32)
  5. The people must stop saying, “The burden of Yahweh” (33–40)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 23:5–6 and 23:9–24.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Shepherds and the flock

Calling rulers “shepherds” and the people they govern “the sheep of my pasture” was a customary way of speaking. Because these shepherds scattered the flock, Yahweh promises to gather the remnant himself and to appoint faithful ones in their place.

### The righteous branch

In 23:5–6 Yahweh promises a king descended from David, the word “branch” picturing a new shoot growing from the stump of David’s dynasty. The name given to him, “Yahweh is our righteousness,” stands in deliberate contrast to King Zedekiah, whose name means “Yahweh is my righteousness.”

### Standing in Yahweh’s counsel

In 23:18 and 23:22, a true prophet is one who has stood in Yahweh’s counsel, that is, one whom Yahweh has admitted to hear his decisions. The prophets Jeremiah opposes have not been there, so what they announce comes from their own hearts and dreams.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The burden of Yahweh

In 23:33–40 the argument turns on one Hebrew word that means both “a message that a prophet carries” and “a heavy load,” which the people were using mockingly. If your language has no single word with both senses, translate the sense that fits each occurrence and consider explaining the wordplay in a footnote.

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s speech is repeatedly interrupted by the formula “the declaration of Yahweh,” and in 23:33–40 quotations are nested several layers deep. If this would confuse your readers, you may translate some inner quotations as indirect quotations.

### Parallelism

The poetry of this chapter often states an idea in one line and restates it in a similar way in the next; if your readers would think the second line makes a separate point, you may combine such pairs.

# Jeremiah 24 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter reports a vision that Yahweh gave to Jeremiah and the explanation that Yahweh attached to it. It is written as prose, not poetry.

  1. Yahweh shows Jeremiah two baskets of figs at the temple (1–3)
  2. Yahweh explains the good figs: the exiles in Babylon (4–7)
  3. Yahweh explains the bad figs: Zedekiah and those who remain (8–10)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The deportation to Babylon

Verse 1 refers to the earlier deportation in which Nebuchadnezzar took King Jeconiah, the officials, and the skilled workers from Jerusalem to Babylon and left Zedekiah ruling over the people who stayed behind.

### The first ripe figs

The figs that ripened earliest in the season were prized as the choicest fruit, so the comparison in verse 2 marks the good figs as the very best.

### A reversal of expectations

The people remaining in Jerusalem would have assumed that they were the ones whom Yahweh had spared, but Yahweh declares the opposite: the exiles are the good figs, and the remnant left in the land are the bad ones.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The figs as an extended comparison

The two baskets of figs stand for two groups of people, and the comparison runs through the whole chapter. Translate the wording about the good figs and the bad figs consistently in verses 2–3, 5, and 8 so that readers can follow the connection between the vision and its explanation.

### Quotations within quotations

Beginning in verse 5, Jeremiah quotes Yahweh, and inside that quotation Yahweh introduces his own words again. If nested quotations would be confusing in your language, you could translate the inner material as an indirect quotation.

# Jeremiah 25 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter gathers up the message of the first half of the book and widens it: because the people have refused to listen for 23 years, Yahweh will bring Babylon against Judah, and afterward he will judge Babylon and every other nation as well.

  1. Jeremiah recalls 23 years of warnings that the people refused to heed (1–7)
  2. Yahweh announces that Babylon will devastate the land for 70 years and that Babylon will then be punished (8–14)
    1. The coming destruction of Judah (8–11)
    2. The later punishment of Babylon (12–14)
  3. Jeremiah makes the nations drink the cup of Yahweh’s wrath (15–29)
    1. Yahweh gives Jeremiah the cup (15–17)
    2. The list of the nations that must drink (18–26)
    3. The message Jeremiah is to speak as they drink (27–29)
  4. A poetic oracle of worldwide judgment (30–38)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 25:30–38.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The seventy years

Yahweh sets a fixed term of 70 years during which the nations will serve the king of Babylon, after which he will punish Babylon itself (25:11–12). The number presents the exile both as a real punishment and as one whose limit Yahweh himself has set.

### The cup of wrath

In the ancient Near East, a cup of wine handed to someone by a superior pictured a fate that the person had to accept. Here the wine in the cup is Yahweh’s wrath, and the nations that drink it stagger, vomit, and fall, images of the confusion and ruin that war will bring.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Sheshach

In 25:26, the name “Sheshach” is a coded way of writing “Babylon” in which each letter of the name is replaced by another letter. Translators may keep the name in the text and explain it in a note, since the list makes clear that Babylon is meant.

### Quotations within quotations

Jeremiah reports Yahweh’s words at length in this chapter, and Yahweh in turn quotes what he said to the people and what Jeremiah is to say to the nations, so that quotations are nested two and three levels deep. The phrase “the declaration of Yahweh” also interrupts speech that Yahweh is himself speaking, and translators may need to mark the boundaries of each quotation clearly or to report some of the speech indirectly.

### Shepherds and the flock

In 25:34–38, the rulers of the nations are called “shepherd” and “nobles of the flock,” and their people are the flock. If this image would be confusing, translators may make the comparison explicit or state plainly that these are rulers and their people.

# Jeremiah 26 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is narrative rather than poetry. It tells how Jeremiah preached a short warning in the temple courtyard, was put on trial for his life and spared, while another prophet who said the same thing was executed.

  1. Yahweh sends Jeremiah to the temple courtyard to warn Judah to turn from evil (1–6)
  2. The priests, the prophets, and the people seize Jeremiah and demand his death (7–11)
  3. Jeremiah answers the officials and the people (12–15)
  4. The officials, the people, and the elders rule that Jeremiah should not die (16–19)
  5. The death of the prophet Uriah, and Ahikam’s protection of Jeremiah (20–24)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the quotation from the prophet Micah in 26:18.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Shiloh and the temple

Shiloh was the place where the house of Yahweh stood before the temple was built in Jerusalem and it, Shiloh, was destroyed. Many in Judah believed that Yahweh would never allow his own temple to be harmed, so the threat that this house would become like Shiloh (26:6) is what provoked the crowd to seize Jeremiah.

### Yahweh relenting

Three times in this chapter (26:3, 26:13, and 26:19) Yahweh relents or holds back concerning a disaster he had announced, because people turn from their evil ways. The point is not that Yahweh changes his character but that his announced judgment is a warning people may still escape.

### Prophecy and the death penalty

The law of Moses required that a prophet who spoke in Yahweh’s name without being sent by him be put to death. The trial in this chapter turns on that question, and the elders settle it by recalling that Hezekiah did not kill the prophet Micah for saying the same thing.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Yahweh’s message to Jeremiah contains the words that Jeremiah is to speak to the people (26:2–6), and later speakers quote Jeremiah’s words and Micah’s words back to one another (26:9 and 26:18). These quotations run two and three levels deep, so translators may need to mark each level clearly or report some of the speech indirectly.

### Innocent blood

In 26:15, Jeremiah warns that killing him would put “innocent blood” on his hearers and on their city. The expression refers to the guilt that comes from killing someone who has done no wrong, not to the blood itself.

# Jeremiah 27 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is narrative rather than poetry. Jeremiah wears a yoke as a sign and delivers one message to three audiences in turn—the envoys of the neighboring nations, King Zedekiah, and the priests and the people: submit to Babylon and live.

  1. Yahweh tells Jeremiah to make a yoke and to send word to the kings of the neighboring nations (1–4)
  2. The message for the nations: Yahweh has handed these lands over to Nebuchadnezzar (5–11)
    1. Yahweh, who made the earth, gives it to whomever he chooses (5–7)
    2. Nations that refuse the yoke will perish; nations that submit will remain on their land (8–11)
  3. The message for Zedekiah king of Judah (12–15)
  4. The message for the priests and the people about the vessels of the temple (16–22)
    1. Do not believe the prophets who promise that the vessels will soon return (16–18)
    2. The vessels that remain will also go to Babylon, and Yahweh will later restore them (19–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The yoke

A yoke was a wooden frame fastened over the necks of oxen so that they could pull a plow together. Jeremiah wears one in order to act out his message, and throughout the chapter putting one’s neck into the yoke of the king of Babylon means accepting his rule and serving him.

### Nebuchadnezzar as Yahweh’s servant

Yahweh calls a pagan king “my servant” (27:6) because Yahweh, as the one who made the earth, gives lands to whomever he chooses; the title says nothing about the king’s loyalty to Yahweh.

### The vessels of the house of Yahweh

These were the pillars, the Sea, the stands, and the other objects made for worship in the temple. Some had already been carried to Babylon when Jeconiah was exiled, and the prophets whom Jeremiah opposes were claiming that they would soon be brought back.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### The date in verse 1

The Hebrew text says that this word came in the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim, but the events of the chapter take place under Zedekiah (27:3 and 27:12). The ULT keeps the Hebrew reading and explains the difficulty in a footnote.

### Quotations within quotations

Jeremiah reports what Yahweh said to him, Yahweh’s words contain the message that the envoys are to carry to their masters, and that message in turn quotes what the false prophets are saying, so that quotations run three and four levels deep. The phrase “the declaration of Yahweh” also interrupts speech that Yahweh is himself speaking (27:8, 27:11, and 27:22), and translators may need to mark the boundaries of each level clearly or to report some of the speech indirectly.

# Jeremiah 28 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a narrative account of a confrontation between Jeremiah and a rival prophet, and it continues the yoke sign that Jeremiah performed in Jeremiah 27. It is prose throughout, with no poetry.

  1. Hananiah predicts that the exile will end within two years (1–4)
  2. Jeremiah answers and states how a true prophet can be recognized (5–9)
    1. Jeremiah says that he wishes Hananiah’s words were true (5–6)
    2. Jeremiah appeals to the pattern of the earlier prophets (7–9)
  3. Hananiah breaks the yoke bar off Jeremiah’s neck (10–11)
  4. Yahweh sends Jeremiah back with a message about iron yoke bars and about Hananiah’s death (12–16)
  5. Hananiah dies that same year (17)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The yoke as a sign

A yoke is a wooden bar that harnesses animals so that they must pull wherever their owner directs them. Jeremiah wore a yoke bar to show that Yahweh had placed the nations under the rule of Nebuchadnezzar, and Hananiah broke that bar to claim the opposite. Both men acted out their messages rather than only speaking them.

### Recognizing a true prophet

Jeremiah argues that a prophet who announces peace is shown to be sent by Yahweh only when his words actually come about, whereas the earlier prophets consistently announced war, disaster, and plague. Hananiah’s death in the same year settles which of the two men Yahweh had sent.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Both prophets introduce their messages with “Thus says Yahweh,” and the narrator reports their words, so speech in this chapter is nested as many as four levels deep. If nested quotations would be confusing in your language, you could translate some of the inner levels as indirect speech.

### Two speakers who both claim to speak for Yahweh

The narrative calls both men “the prophet,” and each one quotes Yahweh directly. Make it clear in each verse which man is speaking, especially in verses 5–6 and 10–11, so that readers do not attribute Hananiah’s claims to Jeremiah.

# Jeremiah 29 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is prose. It records a letter that Jeremiah sent from Jerusalem to the Judeans whom Nebuchadnezzar had already deported to Babylon, and it records what happened when that letter reached them.

  1. The setting of the letter and the men who carried it (1–3)
  2. Jeremiah’s letter to the exiles (4–14)
    1. Instructions to settle down in Babylon (4–7)
    2. Warning against the prophets and diviners among the exiles (8–9)
    3. Promise of return after seventy years (10–14)
  3. Yahweh’s judgment on those still living in Jerusalem (15–19)
  4. Yahweh’s judgment on Ahab and Zedekiah, who prophesy falsely in Babylon (20–23)
  5. Shemaiah’s letter against Jeremiah and Yahweh’s reply (24–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The two groups of Judeans

The people whom this letter addresses had been carried away to Babylon with King Jeconiah, while other Judeans remained in Jerusalem under King Zedekiah. Much of the chapter turns on the contrast between these two groups, since Yahweh promises a future to those already in exile but announces disaster on those who stayed behind.

### False prophecy

Several men in this chapter speak in Yahweh’s name although he did not send them, and the exiles are consulting dreams and diviners as well. Yahweh treats such false prophecy as rebellion against himself and punishes it severely.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

The chapter layers direct speech several levels deep: the narrator quotes Jeremiah’s letter, the letter quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh quotes what other people have said. In 29:25–28 the layering reaches four levels, because Yahweh quotes Shemaiah’s letter, which in turn quotes Jeremiah’s letter. If nested quotation marks would confuse your readers, you could express the inner layers as indirect quotations.

### “The declaration of Yahweh”

This formula interrupts quoted speech at many points in the chapter, including in the middle of sentences. If placing it there would be unnatural in your language, you could move it to the beginning or the end of the sentence that it interrupts.

# Jeremiah 30 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter opens the section often called the Book of Consolation (Jeremiah 30–33), in which Yahweh tells Jeremiah to write down promises of restoration for Israel and Judah. Verses 1–4 are prose, and the rest of the chapter is poetry that moves back and forth between announcing terrible distress and announcing rescue from it.

  1. Yahweh tells Jeremiah to write in a scroll his promise to restore his people (1–3)
  2. The day of distress for Jacob and his rescue from it (4–11)
    1. Terror that is like the pains of childbirth (4–7)
    2. Yahweh breaks the yoke and tells Jacob not to fear (8–11)
  3. The incurable wound that Yahweh has inflicted on his people (12–15)
  4. Yahweh heals the wound and restores the city (16–22)
    1. Those who devoured his people become plunder themselves (16–17)
    2. The city, the community, and their own ruler are restored (18–22)
  5. The storm of Yahweh’s wrath against the wicked (23–24)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 30:5–24.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Restoring the captivity

Yahweh promises to bring his people back from the lands where he scattered them and to give them again the land that he gave to their ancestors. This reversal shapes the whole chapter, and it extends to the city, the palace, the community, and its leadership.

### Breaking the yoke

A yoke was a wooden frame fastened over the necks of oxen to make them pull where their owner directed. Here it pictures the rule of a foreign empire over Yahweh’s people, so breaking the yoke and tearing off the bonds means ending that domination.

### David their king

Yahweh promises that his people will serve “David their king.” David had died long before Jeremiah’s time, so this refers to a future ruler descended from him, the ruler who, in verse 21, comes from among the people themselves.

### You will be my people

The words “you will be to me for a people, and I will be to you for God” in verse 22 are a standard way of stating the covenant relationship between Yahweh and his people.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Interrupted speech and shifting speakers

Yahweh’s words are repeatedly broken into by the phrase “the declaration of Yahweh,” which is the narrator’s comment, rather than part of what Yahweh says, and Yahweh sometimes speaks of himself in the third person. If this would confuse your readers, you could move such phrases to the beginning or end of the sentence or make them a separate sentence.

### Names for the people of God

The chapter addresses the people as “Jacob,” “Israel,” and “Zion,” and it speaks of them at times as a single, wounded person, switching between singular and plural forms. It may help to make clear in each place that a group of people is meant.

### Parallelism

The poetry of this chapter often states an idea in one line and then restates it in a similar way in the next line, so the two lines should not sound like two separate events.

# Jeremiah 31 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the section often called the Book of Consolation (Jeremiah 30-33). Most of it is poetry in which Yahweh promises to gather his scattered people, to turn their mourning into joy, and to make a new covenant with them, and prose paragraphs frame the poems at verses 1–2, 23–28, and 38–40.

  1. Yahweh loves Israel and brings his scattered people home (1–14)
    1. Everlasting love and the rebuilding of virgin Israel (1–6)
    2. Yahweh gathers the remnant from the land of the north (7–11)
    3. Mourning turned to joy and plenty in Zion (12–14)
  2. Rachel’s weeping ends and Ephraim returns (15–22)
    1. Rachel refuses to be comforted, and Yahweh promises a reward (15–17)
    2. Ephraim repents and Yahweh has compassion on him (18–20)
    3. A call to set up signposts and return home (21–22)
  3. Judah and its cities dwell in the land again (23–26)
  4. Yahweh replants his people, and each person dies for his own sin (27–30)
  5. Yahweh makes a new covenant with Israel and Judah (31–34)
  6. Yahweh swears that Israel will endure, and the city is rebuilt (35–40)
    1. As sure as the sun, the moon, and the stars (35–37)
    2. Jerusalem rebuilt and holy to Yahweh (38–40)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 31:3–6, 31:8–22, and 31:29–37.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The new covenant

In verses 31–34 Yahweh promises a covenant that will not be like the one he made when he brought Israel out of Egypt. He will put his law within his people and write it on their hearts, everyone will know him without having to be taught, and he will forgive their iniquity and remember their sin no longer.

### Rachel weeping for her sons

Rachel was the ancestor of the northern tribes through Joseph, so here she stands for the mothers of those tribes. The prophet pictures her weeping at Ramah, a town north of Jerusalem on the road along which captives were taken away, because her descendants have been carried off into exile.

### Ephraim

Ephraim was the leading tribe of the northern kingdom, so its name stands for that whole kingdom. Yahweh speaks of Ephraim as his firstborn son, a son whom he has disciplined, who has repented, and who is still precious to him.

### Sour grapes and blunt teeth

The saying quoted in verse 29 was a complaint that children suffered punishment for what their parents had done. Yahweh says that his people will no longer use this saying, because each person will die for his own iniquity.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Interrupted speech and shifting speakers

Yahweh’s words are repeatedly broken into by the phrase “the declaration of Yahweh,” which is the narrator’s comment rather than part of what Yahweh says, and there are quotations within quotations in several places. The prophet also speaks in his own voice at times, as in verse 26. If this would confuse your readers, you could move such phrases to the beginning or end of the sentence, make clear who is speaking, or express some of the inner quotations as indirect speech.

### Israel pictured as a woman

Yahweh addresses his people as “virgin of Israel” and “apostate daughter,” and he speaks of them adorning themselves with tambourines and going out in the dance. These images present the whole nation as a young woman, so the singular “you” in these verses refers to the people as a group rather than to one person.

# Jeremiah 32 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter combines narrative, a prophetic sign-act, a prayer, and two oracles. It stands at the center of the book’s message of hope: at the very moment Jerusalem is about to fall, Jeremiah buys a field as a pledge that Yahweh will restore his people to the land.

1. Yahweh’s word comes to Jeremiah while he is confined during the siege of Jerusalem (32:1–5)
2. Jeremiah buys his cousin’s field at Anathoth and preserves the deed as a sign (32:6–15)
    1. Hanamel offers the field and Jeremiah completes the purchase (32:6–12)
    2. Jeremiah instructs Baruch to store the documents (32:13–15)
3. Jeremiah prays, praising Yahweh’s power and asking about the purchase (32:16–25)
4. Yahweh answers that the city will indeed fall because of Judah’s idolatry (32:26–35)
5. Yahweh promises to gather his people, make an everlasting covenant with them, and see fields bought again (32:36–44)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The right of redemption

Israelite law gave the nearest relative both the right and the duty to buy a family member’s land so that the property would remain within the clan. Jeremiah’s purchase of Hanamel’s field is a legal transaction of this kind, so translate it in a way that shows Jeremiah was obligated as well as entitled to buy.

### Sealed and open deeds

When land changed hands, the terms were recorded twice: one copy was rolled up and sealed so that no one could alter it, and a second copy was left open so that it could be read. Placing both in an earthenware jar preserved the legal record for many years.

### Worship of Baal and Molech

Verses 29–35 list the practices that provoked Yahweh to anger: burning offerings to Baal on the flat roofs of houses, and sacrificing children at the high places in the Valley of Ben Hinnom to Molech.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### A sign-act and its explanation

The purchase in verses 6–15 is a symbolic action, not merely a family matter, and Yahweh explains it in verses 42–44. Translate the buying, writing, sealing, and witnessing language consistently in both places so that readers can see that the promise answers the sign.

### Quotations within quotations

Speech is layered repeatedly in this chapter: Yahweh’s words are within Jeremiah’s report, contained in the narrator’s account, and in verses 36 and 43, the people’s own words are quoted back to them. If such nesting is confusing in your language, you may render the inner layers as indirect quotations.

### Idioms for anger and stubbornness

Hebrew describes Yahweh’s anger with physical images, such as this city being “to my nose and to my heat” in verse 31, and pictures the people’s rebellion as turning “the neck and not the face” in verse 33. Express these ideas in a way that is natural in your language.

# Jeremiah 33 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the section of hope in chapters 30–33. Yahweh gives Jeremiah a second message while the prophet is still confined in the courtyard of the guard during the Babylonian siege, and the message moves from the ruined city to a promise of healing, joy, and an enduring king and priesthood.

  1. Jeremiah’s location when Yahweh gave him a second message (1)
  2. Yahweh’s recitation of things about who he is and his invitation to Jeremiah to call on him for things he does not know (2-3)
  3. Yahweh turns the city from judgment to healing and forgiveness (4–11)
  4. Shepherds and flocks fill the pastures again (12–13)
  5. Yahweh promises a righteous branch for David and an enduring priesthood (14–18)
  6. Yahweh’s covenant with day and night secures his promises (19–26)
    1. If the covenant with day and night could be broken (19–22)
    2. Yahweh answers those who say he has rejected his people (23–26)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### A future restoration

Three times Yahweh promises to undo what the exile has done to his people, rendered “restore the restoration” in 33:7 and 33:11 and “return their restoration” in 33:26. The Hebrew expression pictures giving a people back everything they had lost, and it frames the chapter’s hope of a future restoration for God’s covenant people.

### The branch of David and the Levitical priests

Verses 14–26 join Yahweh’s promise of a future ruler from David’s line to the continuing service of the Levite priests who present burnt offerings and grain offerings. Both promises rest on a covenant that Yahweh says is as unbreakable as the fixed order of day and night.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Nearly the whole chapter is Yahweh’s direct speech, and within it Yahweh quotes what other people say, sometimes to a third level, as in 33:10 and 33:24. If layered quotations would confuse your readers, you may translate the inner ones as indirect quotations.

### “A man will not be cut off”

This idiom in 33:17 and 33:18 means that David’s royal line and the priestly line will never lack someone to fill their role. Translate it in a way that expresses ongoing succession rather than physical harm.

# Jeremiah 34 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is narrative and records two messages that Yahweh gave during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem. The first is a message to King Zedekiah regarding what will happen to him and the cities of Judah, and the second message condemns the people of Jerusalem for freeing their Hebrew slaves and then forcing them back into slavery.

  1. Yahweh warns Zedekiah that Jerusalem will fall to Babylon (1–7)
    1. Zedekiah will be captured and taken to Babylon (1–3)
    2. Zedekiah will die in peace and be mourned (4–5)
    3. Jeremiah delivers the message while the army of Babylon attacks the cities of Judah (6–7)
  2. The people free their Hebrew slaves and then take them back (8–11)
  3. Yahweh condemns the people for breaking the covenant (12–22)
    1. Yahweh reminds them of the law of release that their ancestors ignored (12–16)
    2. Yahweh announces punishment on those who broke the covenant (17–21)
    3. The Babylonian army will return and capture and burn the city (22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The release of Hebrew slaves

The law of Moses required that an Israelite who had to sell himself as a slave to a fellow Israelite be set free after six years of service (see Exodus 21:2 and Deuteronomy 15:12). The people of Judah had neglected this law, obeyed it briefly, and then broke their promise.

### Passing between the pieces of a calf

In 34:18–19, the people made a covenant by cutting a calf in two and walking between the halves. This ritual meant that those who passed between the pieces were calling on themselves the same fate as the animal if they broke their promise (compare Genesis 15:9–17).

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Ironic use of “freedom”

In 34:17, Yahweh uses the same word “freedom” that described the release of the slaves, but now he “proclaims freedom” to the sword, the plague, and the famine. Translate this in a way that keeps the connection between the freedom the people refused to give and the punishment they will receive.

# Jeremiah 35 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a narrative that Jeremiah tells mostly in the first person. It takes place during the reign of King Jehoiakim, so it is earlier than the events of chapters 32–34, which happened under King Zedekiah. Yahweh uses the faithfulness of the Rechabites to their ancestor’s commands as an object lesson to show how unfaithful the people of Judah have been to him.

1. Jeremiah offers wine to the Rechabites in a temple chamber in obedience to Yahweh’s command (1–5)
2. The Rechabites refuse to drink because of their ancestor’s commands (6–10)
3. Why the Rechabites came to Jerusalem (11)
4. Yahweh contrasts the obedience of the Rechabites with the disobedience of Judah and announces disaster on Judah (12–17)
5. Yahweh promises that the descendants of Jonadab will always serve him (18–19)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The Rechabites

The Rechabites were a family group descended from Jonadab son of Rechab, who helped King Jehu destroy the worship of Baal in Israel about 250 years earlier (see 2 Kings 10:15–23). Jonadab commanded his descendants not to drink wine, build houses, or farm, but to live in tents like people who were not settled in the land. They had moved into Jerusalem only to escape the invading Babylonian army.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Listening as obeying

This chapter repeatedly uses the word “listen” to mean “obey.” This word contrasts the Rechabites, who “listened” to Jonadab, with the people of Judah, who did not “listen” to Yahweh. If possible, translate this word consistently so that readers can see the contrast.

### Quotations within quotations

Jeremiah reports what the Rechabites said, and they quote Jonadab (6–7) and themselves (11). Jeremiah also reports messages from Yahweh that contain further quotations (13–17). If it would be clearer in your language, you could translate some of these as indirect quotations. See: [Quotes within Quotes](ta:figs-quotesinquotes)

# Jeremiah 36 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a historical narrative set during the reign of King Jehoiakim. It tells how Jeremiah’s prophecies were written on a scroll, how the king destroyed that scroll, and how Yahweh instructed Jeremiah to make another one.

1. Yahweh commands Jeremiah to write down all his messages on a scroll (1–3)
2. Baruch writes the scroll and reads it at the temple (4–10)
    1. Jeremiah dictates the words and sends Baruch to read them (4–7)
    2. Baruch reads the scroll to the people on a day of fasting (8-10)
3. The officials hear the scroll and tell Baruch and Jeremiah to hide (11–19)
4. King Jehoiakim burns the scroll (20–25)
5. The king tries to capture Jeremiah and Baruch but Yahweh hides them (26)
6. Yahweh announces judgment on Jehoiakim and has the scroll written again (27–32)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Scrolls and scribes

A scroll was a long strip of leather or papyrus on which a scribe wrote in columns with ink and which was then rolled up. Because Jeremiah was not able to go to the temple, he dictated his messages to Baruch, who wrote them down and read them aloud for him.

### Fasting and tearing garments

The people gathered at the temple for a day of fasting to ask Yahweh for mercy 36:9. Tearing one’s garments was a public sign of grief and/or repentance, so the statement in 36:24 that the king and his servants did not do this shows that they refused to take Yahweh’s warning seriously.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “Scroll” and “scroll of a book”

The chapter refers to the same written document, the first scroll, as both a “scroll” and a “scroll of a book.” Your translation should make clear that these refer to one object.

### Listening as obeying

In this chapter the word “listen” means “obey” both times it occurs. If possible, translate this word consistently so that readers can see the reoccurring theme. See the the translation note at the first occurrence in this chapter, verse 25, for translation guidance.

### “Word” and “Words” meaning “message” or “messages”

This chapter repeatedly uses the words “word” and “words” to refer to a “message” or “messages.” If possible, translate this word consistently so that readers can see the reoccurring theme. See the the translations note in verse 1 for “this word was to Jeremiah from Yahweh” and in verse 2 for “all the words” for translation guidance.

### Jeremiah speaking about himself

Jeremiah wrote this account, but he refers to himself in the third person throughout the chapter. If this would be confusing in your language, you could use the first person, as the UST does.

### Time references

This chapter moves from the fourth year of Jehoiakim ([36:1](ta:36)) to the ninth month of his fifth year (36:9). Make sure these time markers are clear in your translation so that readers understand that Baruch read the scroll in public some time after Yahweh first told Jeremiah to write it.

# Jeremiah 37 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a narrative set during the final siege of Jerusalem in the reign of King Zedekiah. It moves back in time from the events of chapters 35–36, which took place during the reign of Zedekiah’s brother Jehoiakim.

1. Zedekiah asks Jeremiah to pray for the people (1–5)
2. Yahweh’s message that the Chaldeans will return and burn Jerusalem (6–10)
3. Jeremiah is arrested and imprisoned (11–16)
4. Zedekiah consults Jeremiah in secret (17–21)
    1. Jeremiah tells the king that he will be handed over to the king of Babylon (17)
    2. Jeremiah declares his own innocence and reminds the king that the false prophets had prophesied untrue things (18-19)
    3. Jeremiah asks not to be sent back to prison and is moved to the courtyard of the guard (20–21)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The temporary lifting of the siege

The army of the Chaldeans had surrounded Jerusalem, but it withdrew for a time when the army of Pharaoh came out of Egypt. Many people in Jerusalem hoped that this meant the danger was over, but Yahweh told Jeremiah that the Chaldeans would come back and destroy the city.

### Deserting to the enemy

Jeremiah had told the people that those who surrendered to the Chaldeans would live (see Jeremiah 21:9). For this reason, when he tried to leave the city, the guard at the gate accused him of deserting to the enemy, and the officials treated him as a traitor.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Jeremiah referred to in the third person

This chapter refers to Jeremiah in the third person, as “Jeremiah” or “Jeremiah the prophet,” even though he is the prophet whose words this book records. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the first person, as the UST does.

### Places where Jeremiah was held

This chapter mentions several places where Jeremiah was held: the house of Jonathan the scribe, which was being used as a prison, the cistern house and its cells, and the courtyard of the guard.

# Jeremiah 38 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a narrative that continues the events of chapter 37 during the Babylonian siege of Jerusalem under King Zedekiah.

1. The officials have Jeremiah thrown into a cistern (1–6)
    1. Jeremiah tells the people that Yahweh says that those who surrender to the Chaldeans will live (1–3)
    2. The officials accuse Jeremiah, and the king hands him over to them and they put Jeremiah into a cistern (4–6)
2. Ebed Melech rescues Jeremiah from the cistern (7–13)
3. Zedekiah consults Jeremiah in secret (14–23)
    1. Zedekiah promises with an oath not to harm Jeremiah (14–16)
    2. Jeremiah urges Zedekiah to surrender to the Babylonians and tells him what the consequences will be if he does not (17–23)
4. Zedekiah tells Jeremiah to keep their conversation secret (24–27)
5. Jeremiah remains in the courtyard of the guard until Jerusalem is captured (28)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the song of the women in 38:22.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Cisterns

A cistern was a deep pit dug into rock to collect and store rainwater, with a narrow opening at the top. Because this cistern held only mud, and because it was deep with vertical walls with nothing to hold onto, Jeremiah could not climb out and he would have died there from hunger and exposure if no one had rescued him

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Jeremiah described in the third person

As in chapter 37, this chapter refers to Jeremiah in the third person even though he is the prophet whose words this book records. If it would be clearer in your language, you could use the first person.

### “Hand” meaning power or control

The chapter often uses the word “hand” to refer to someone’s power or control, as in being given “into the hand of” the Chaldeans. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this meaning plainly.

### “Going out” and “go out” meaning “surrender to”

This chapter often uses the phrases “going out” and “go out” to refer to surrendering. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express this meaning plainly.

# Jeremiah 39 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a historical narrative that tells how the army of Babylon conquered Jerusalem, just as Jeremiah had prophesied, and what then happened to Zedekiah, to the people, to Jeremiah, and to Ebed Melech.

1. The Babylonian army besieges and breaks into Jerusalem (1–3)
2. Zedekiah flees, but is captured and punished at Riblah (4–7)
3. The Babylonians burn Jerusalem and take most the people into exile (8–9)
4. The poor people who did not own anything are left in Judah (10)
5. Nebuchadnezzar has Jeremiah released and entrusted to Gedaliah (11–14)
6. Yahweh’s earlier promise to rescue Ebed Melech (15–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The fulfillment of Jeremiah’s prophecies

The events of this chapter are what Jeremiah had repeatedly warned would happen if Zedekiah and the people did not surrender to Babylon (38:17–23). Yahweh had used the Chaldeans to punish Judah by sending its people into exile. Verses 1–10 tell the same events as 2 Kings 25:1–12 and Jeremiah 52:4–16.

### Yahweh rewards those who trust him

Jeremiah 38:7–13 records that Ebed Melech rescued Jeremiah from the cistern. Jeremiah 39:15–18 recounts Yahweh’s earlier promise to spare Ebed Melech’s life because he had trusted in Yahweh and delivered Jeremiah from dying in the cistern.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Babylonian names and titles

Verses 3 and 13 list Babylonian officials. The words “Rabsaris” and “Rabmag,” are titles rather than personal names. There are different opinions among Bible scholars on the exact meaning of these two titles.

### Background information in verses 15–18

Verses 15–18 describe a message Yahweh had given to Jeremiah earlier, while he was still confined in the courtyard of the guard, before the city fell. Make it clear in your translation that these events happened before the events of verses 11–14. The UST for verse 15 provides one possible way to do that.

# Jeremiah 40 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is a historical narrative that tells what happened in Judah after Babylon conquered Jerusalem. It begins the account of the people who remained in the land under the governor Gedaliah, which continues through chapter 44.

  1. The captain of the guards releases Jeremiah (1–6)
    1. The captain explains why the disaster happened (1–3)
    2. The captain lets Jeremiah choose where to go (4–5)
    3. Jeremiah goes to Gedaliah at Mizpah (6)
  2. Gedaliah governs the people who remain in Judah (7–12)
    1. The army captains come to Gedaliah, and he urges them to serve Babylon (7–10)
    2. Jews from other lands return to Judah (11–12)
  3. Johanan warns Gedaliah about Ishmael’s plot (13–16)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The remnant left in Judah

The king of Babylon took most of the people into exile, but he left the poorest people in the land and appointed Gedaliah to govern them from Mizpah. These people, together with soldiers who had escaped and Jews who returned from nearby lands, made up the remnant of people who lived in the land of Judah.

### A Babylonian official speaks of Yahweh

In verses 2–3, Nebuzaradan, a Babylonian official, says that Yahweh brought the disaster on Jerusalem because the people sinned against him. This repeats what Jeremiah had warned all along, so the captain is acknowledging that Jeremiah’s prophecies were true.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### “The word that was to Jeremiah”

Verse 1 begins the way Jeremiah’s prophecies usually do, but no message from Yahweh follows right away. The phrase probably introduces the whole account in chapters 40–44, which leads up to the message Yahweh gives in 42:7–22.

### Jeremiah’s second release

Jeremiah 39:11-14 says that the Babylonians released Jeremiah from the courtyard of the guard and entrusted him to Gedaliah and that Jeremiah then lived in his own house among the people of Judah. That was the first time that Jeremiah was released. Jeremiah 40:1-5 records the second time that Jeremiah was released. It recounts that Jeremiah was chained among the Jewish captives who were being held at Ramah when Nebuzaradan released him. What probably happened is that, after Jeremiah’s first release, Babylonian soldiers mistakenly gathered Jeremiah along with the other captives who were being sent to Ramah before being sent to Babylon. While Jeremiah was at Ramah, Nebuzaradan recognized him and set him free for the second time. Make sure your translation does not present Jeremiah 39:11-14 and Jeremiah 40:1-5 as conflicting accounts.

# Jeremiah 41 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the historical account from chapter 40 of what happened in Judah after the Babylonian army captured Jerusalem.

1. Ishmael murders Gedaliah and the people with him at Mizpah (1–3)
2. Ishmael murders the men who came to worship (4–9)
3. Ishmael takes the people of Mizpah captive (10)
4. Johanan rescues the captives, and Ishmael escapes to Ammon (11–15)
5. Johanan and the people prepare to flee to Egypt (16–18)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Eating together as a sign of friendship

In this culture, eating a meal with someone showed friendship and loyalty. When Ishmael and his men ate with Gedaliah (verse 1) and then killed him (verse 2), that was a serious betrayal.

### Signs of mourning

The 80 men in verse 5 had shaved their beards, torn their clothes, and cut themselves. These were signs that they were mourning, probably because the temple had been destroyed. They were still bringing a grain offering and frankincense to the place where the house of Yahweh (Yahweh’s temple) had stood.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Many participants with long names

The chapter repeatedly identifies people by name and father’s name, such as “Ishmael, the son of Nethaniah” and “Johanan, the son of Kareah.” If repeating these full names would be unnatural in your language, you could use the full name only where it is needed to make clear who is acting.

# Jeremiah 42 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the historical account from chapters 40–41. The people who remain in Judah ask Jeremiah what Yahweh wants them to do, and Yahweh tells them not to go to Egypt.

  1. The people ask Jeremiah to pray for guidance (1–6)
    1. The leaders and people ask Jeremiah to pray to Yahweh for them (1–3)
    2. Jeremiah agrees, and the people promise to obey (4–6)
  2. Yahweh promises to protect them if they stay in Judah (7–12)
  3. Yahweh warns that they will die if they go to Egypt (13–18)
  4. Jeremiah warns the people that they will not obey (19–22)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### An oath calling Yahweh as witness

In verse 5, the people make an oath that Yahweh would be a true and faithful witness against them if they did not do everything he told them. This means they were asking Yahweh to punish them if they broke their promise.

### Going down to Egypt

Johanan and the remnant of Judah wanted to go to Egypt because they were afraid that the king of Babylon would punish them for Ishmael’s murder of Gedaliah. Yahweh tells them that staying in Judah under his protection is safe, but going to Egypt will bring the very disasters they are trying to escape.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

In verses 10–19, Jeremiah quotes what Yahweh said, and Yahweh in turn quotes what the people were saying. In verses 13-14 Jeremiah quotes Yahweh saying two things that the people of Judah might say. In verse 20, Jeremiah quotes the people’s earlier request to him. Make sure that your translation shows clearly who is speaking in each part.

### Who is speaking in verses 19–22

In verses 19-22, Jeremiah speaks to the people directly and stops quoting Yahweh, except to quote Yahweh as saying “Do not go to Egypt” in verse 19. In verses 19-22 Jeremiah tells the people of Judah that they made a fatal mistake when they promised to obey Yahweh but then refused to obey him.
