# Jeremiah 43 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the historical account from chapter 42. The leaders reject Yahweh’s warning and take the people who remain in Judah to Egypt, where Yahweh tells Jeremiah that Babylon will conquer Egypt as well.

  1. The leaders reject Yahweh’s message and go to Egypt (1–7)
    1. The leaders accuse Jeremiah of lying (1–3)
    2. The leaders take the remnant of Judah to Egypt (4–7)
  2. Jeremiah’s symbolic action in Tahpanhes (8–13)
    1. Yahweh tells Jeremiah to hide stones at Pharaoh’s house (8–9)
    2. Yahweh announces that Nebuchadnezzar will conquer Egypt (10–13)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Seeking safety in Egypt

The remnant of Judah went to Egypt to escape the Chaldeans, even though Yahweh had told them that they would be safe only if they stayed in Judah. Yahweh now shows them that Egypt will not protect them, because the king of Babylon will conquer Egypt too.

### Nebuchadnezzar as Yahweh’s servant

In verse 10, Yahweh calls Nebuchadnezzar “my servant.” This does not mean that Nebuchadnezzar worshiped Yahweh. It means that Yahweh was using him to carry out his judgment, including burning the temples of the gods of Egypt.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Symbolic action

In verse 9, Yahweh tells Jeremiah to bury large stones at the entrance of Pharaoh’s house in Tahpanhes. This is a symbolic action that shows that Nebuchadnezzar will set up his throne on that very spot when he conquers Egypt.

### Quotations within quotations

In verse 10, Yahweh tells Jeremiah what to say to the Judeans, and Jeremiah’s message quotes what Yahweh says. Make sure that your translation shows clearly who is speaking in each part.

# Jeremiah 44 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

In this chapter, Jeremiah gives a final message to the Jews living in Egypt, they refuse to listen, and Yahweh confirms his judgment on them.

1. Yahweh’s message to the Jews in Egypt (1–14)
    1. Yahweh reminds them why he destroyed Jerusalem and Judah (1–6)
    2. Yahweh rebukes them for worshiping other gods in Egypt (7–10)
    3. Yahweh announces that he will punish them in Egypt (11–14)
2. The people refuse to listen and defend their worship of the queen of the heavens (15–19)
3. Jeremiah answers that their incense burning is the reason for the disaster (20–23)
4. Yahweh confirms his judgment on the Jews in Egypt (24–30)
    1. Yahweh holds them to their vows and swears an oath against them (24–28)
    2. Yahweh gives the defeat of Pharaoh Hophra as a sign (29–30)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The queen of the heavens

The “queen of the heavens” was a goddess whom people in this region worshiped by burning [incense](tw:incense), pouring out [drinkoffering](tw:drinkoffering)s, and making cakes in her image. The people claim that they prospered while they worshiped her and suffered when they stopped (see 44:17–18). See [falsegod](tw:falsegod).

### The remnant of Judah

The Jews in Egypt were the [remnant](tw:remnant) who survived the Babylonian destruction of Judah and then fled to Egypt against Yahweh’s command. Yahweh says that only a few of them will escape and return to Judah.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Jeremiah quotes Yahweh, and Yahweh in turn quotes his own earlier warnings through the prophets and the people’s vows (see 44:4 and 44:25). Translators may need to use forms in their language that make clear who is speaking at each level.

### Sarcastic command

In 44:25, Yahweh tells the people to perform their vows to the queen of the heavens. He is not approving of these vows but is ironically handing them over to the consequences of what they have chosen.

# Jeremiah 45 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This short chapter is a personal message from Yahweh to Baruch, the scribe who wrote down Jeremiah’s prophecies. It is dated to the fourth year of King Jehoiakim, the same time as the events in [Jeremiah 36:1–4](ta:36), so it is not in chronological order with the chapters around it.

1. Introduction: Jeremiah gives Baruch a message while Baruch is writing down his words (1)
2. Yahweh repeats Baruch’s complaint about his sorrow and weariness (2–3)
3. Yahweh responds to Baruch (4–5)
    1. Yahweh is tearing down what he built and uprooting what he planted (4)
    2. Yahweh tells Baruch not to seek great things, but promises to keep him alive (5)

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Baruch the scribe

[baruch](tw:baruch) was Jeremiah’s helper who wrote down on a [scroll](tw:scroll) the messages that Yahweh gave to Jeremiah. His complaint in this chapter shows the hardship that this work brought him.

### Building and planting

In verse 4, Yahweh uses the language of building, tearing down, planting, and uprooting that he used when he first called Jeremiah in Jeremiah 1:10. It describes how Yahweh established his people and is now removing them because of their sin.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Quotations within quotations

Jeremiah speaks to Baruch, quoting what Yahweh says, and Yahweh in turn quotes Baruch’s own words (3) and tells Jeremiah what to say to Baruch (4–5). Make sure that the speaker of each quotation is clear in your translation.

# Jeremiah 46 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins the section of Jeremiah that contains messages against foreign nations (chapters 46–51). It contains two messages against Egypt, followed by a promise to Israel.

1. Heading for the messages about the nations (1)
2. First message against Egypt: its army is defeated at Carchemish (2–12)
    1. Commands to Egypt’s army and its flight (2–6)
    2. Egypt rises like the Nile, but Yahweh takes vengeance (7–12)
3. Second message against Egypt: Nebuchadnezzar invades Egypt (13–26)
    1. Warning to Egypt’s cities and the flight of its soldiers (13–19)
    2. Pictures of Egypt’s defeat (20–24)
    3. Yahweh punishes Egypt’s gods and rulers (25–26)
4. Yahweh promises to rescue and discipline Israel (27–28)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 46:3–12 and 46:14–24.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### The battle of Carchemish

The first message is dated to the time when the army of Babylon defeated the army of Egypt at Carchemish beside the Euphrates River. The second message speaks of a later time when Nebuchadnezzar would invade Egypt itself. (See: [egypt](tw:egypt) and [babylon](tw:babylon))

### The day of Yahweh as a sacrifice

In 46:10, Jeremiah describes the battle as a day when Yahweh takes vengeance on his enemies, and he speaks of the soldiers who are killed as a sacrifice to Yahweh. (See: [dayofthelord](tw:dayofthelord) and [sacrifice](tw:sacrifice))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changing speakers and audiences

Yahweh is the main speaker, but the poetry often gives commands to Egypt’s army that the soldiers will not be able to obey, and it quotes Egypt (46:8) and foreign soldiers (46:16–17). Make it clear who is speaking and to whom in each part, and mark the quotations within quotations in a way that is natural in your language.

### Egypt pictured as a woman

The chapter speaks of Egypt as the “virgin daughter of Egypt,” the “daughter of Egypt,” and a heifer, and it often uses feminine pronouns for the nation. Use the same images and pronouns consistently throughout the chapter if your language allows.

### Promise to Jacob

The promise in 46:27–28 is nearly the same as the promise in 30:10–11. Consider translating the two passages in the same way.

# Jeremiah 47 General Notes

# Jeremiah 48 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter is Yahweh’s oracle of judgment against Moab, the nation east of the Dead Sea. (See: [moab](tw:moab))

  1. Destruction spreads across the towns of Moab (1–10)
  2. Moab, undisturbed like wine left on its dregs, will be emptied and shamed (11–17)
  3. Judgment comes on the cities of the plateau (18–28)
    1. Dibon, Aroer, and the towns of the plateau fall (18–25)
    2. Moab will become a derision because it mocked Israel (26–28)
  4. Yahweh laments over proud Moab (29–39)
  5. Moab cannot escape, but Yahweh will restore it in the future (40–47)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [48:1–25](ta:48), 48:27–33, and 48:39–47.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Chemosh

Chemosh was the chief god of Moab. Yahweh says that Chemosh will go into exile with his priests and that Moab will be ashamed of him, which shows that this false god cannot protect his people. (See: [falsegod](tw:falsegod))

### Mourning customs

Shaved heads, clipped beards, gashed hands, and sackcloth were ways people in this culture showed deep grief. (See: [mourn](tw:mourn) and [sackcloth](tw:sackcloth))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### References to Moab

The text refers to Moab as “she” and as “he,” and as both singular and plural, sometimes within the same verse. If this would confuse readers, use one pronoun consistently or say “Moab” or “the people of Moab.”

### Place names

The chapter names many towns of Moab, and some of the names sound like Hebrew words that describe what will happen to those towns. Spell the names consistently, and consider explaining the wordplay in a footnote.

### The one who weeps for Moab

It is not always clear whether the “I” who weeps for Moab in 31–36 is Yahweh or Jeremiah. Keep the first person rather than naming the speaker.

### Parallelism

Much of the chapter uses parallel lines that repeat the same idea in different words for emphasis.

# Jeremiah 49 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter continues the series of messages that Yahweh gave Jeremiah against the nations around Judah (46:1–51:64). It contains five separate oracles.

1. Against Ammon (1–6)
2. Against Edom (7–22)
3. Against Damascus (23–27)
4. Against Kedar and the kingdoms of Hazor (28–33)
5. Against Elam (34–39)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [49:1–33](ta:49) and 49:35–39.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Oracles against the nations

Each oracle begins by naming the nation it concerns and repeats phrases such as “thus says Yahweh” and “the declaration of Yahweh.” Translate these repeated formulas consistently throughout the chapter.

### The cup of Yahweh’s anger

In 49:12, drinking a cup represents suffering the punishment that Yahweh gives. Jeremiah used this image earlier when Yahweh made the nations drink the cup of his [wrath](tw:wrath) (Jeremiah 25:15–29).

### Restoring the fortunes

Yahweh promises that after judging Ammon and Elam he will [restore](tw:restore) them (49:6, 49:39). This means that he will make them prosper again, not just bring back captives.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Changes of speaker and addressee

Yahweh speaks for most of the chapter, but the prophet speaks in some places (49:14, 49:20). The oracles also move back and forth between speaking to a nation as “you” and speaking about it as “he” or “she.” Make sure that it is clear who is speaking and to whom.

### Rhetorical questions

Each oracle uses rhetorical questions to rebuke a nation’s pride or to show that no one can resist Yahweh. Consider whether your readers would understand these as statements.

### Parallel with Obadiah

Much of the oracle against Edom (49:9–10, 49:14–16) closely resembles Obadiah 1:1–6. Translators may wish to translate the shared wording similarly in both books.
50:
# Jeremiah 50 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter begins Jeremiah’s last prophecy against a foreign nation, a single message against Babylon that continues through chapter 51.

1. Heading of the prophecy against Babylon (1)
2. Babylon falls and Israel returns to Yahweh (2–20)
    1. Babylon is captured, and Israel and Judah seek Yahweh (2–5)
    2. Yahweh’s lost flock is told to flee from Babylon (6–10)
    3. Babylon is shamed for plundering Yahweh’s people (11–16)
    4. Yahweh punishes Babylon and restores Israel (17–20)
3. Yahweh commands armies to attack Babylon (21–32)
4. Yahweh the Redeemer sends a sword against Babylon (33–40)
5. A nation from the north comes against Babylon by Yahweh’s plan (41–46)

Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in 50:2–46.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Babylon’s gods

Bel and Marduk (50:2) were names for the chief god of Babylon. Saying that these idols are shamed means that they cannot protect Babylon from Yahweh. (See: [falsegod](tw:falsegod))

### Yahweh as Redeemer

In 50:34, Yahweh is called Israel’s “Redeemer.” In Israel, a redeemer was a close relative who defended a family member and set him free from trouble or slavery. (See: [redeem](tw:redeem))

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Future events described as past

Jeremiah often speaks of Babylon’s defeat as if it has already happened, as in “Babylon has been captured” (50:2). This shows that it will certainly happen. If this would confuse your readers, you could use future verb forms.

### Changing addressees

Yahweh speaks to different groups without announcing each change: the nations, the Israelites in Babylon, the Babylonians, the attacking armies, and Babylon itself, which he calls “presumption” (50:31). He alternates between calling Babylon “she” and “he.” Make sure your readers can tell who is being addressed.

### Flock imagery

Throughout the chapter, Israel is pictured as a flock of sheep, its leaders as shepherds, and its homeland as a pasture. (See: [sheep](tw:sheep))

# Jeremiah 51 Introduction

## Structure and Formatting

This chapter completes the long series of prophecies against Babylon that began in chapter 50 and closes the collection of prophecies against the nations. Yahweh summons armies to destroy Babylon, contrasts himself as the maker of the world with Babylon’s lifeless images, and repays the city measure for measure for what it did to Zion. A short prose narrative at the end tells how Jeremiah sent the written prophecy to Babylon.

  1. Yahweh will raise up destroyers against Babylon (1–14)
  2. Yahweh, the maker of the earth, is contrasted with worthless idols (15–19)
  3. Babylon was Yahweh’s war club, but will be repaid for what they did to Zion (20–26)
  4. Nations attack Babylon and it collapses (27–33)
  5. The people of Zion complain and Yahweh avenges them (34–44)
  6. A last call to flee Babylon, and Babylon’s final defeat (45–58)
  7. Jeremiah sends the scroll with Seraiah to Babylon (59–64)

The prophecies are in the form of poetry. Some translations set each line of poetry farther to the right than the rest of the text to make it easier to read. The ULT does this with the poetry in [51:1–58](ta:51), while 51:59–64 is not poetry.

## Religious and Cultural Concepts in This Chapter

### Bel and the images of Babylon

Bel was the chief god of Babylon, and people thought that the city’s greatness was because of him. Yahweh announces that he will punish Bel and make him give back what he stole in 51:44, and that Babylon’s carved and cast images of their gods are lifeless frauds in 51:17–18.

### Vengeance for the temple

Babylon’s punishment is presented as repayment for what it did in Zion, especially for entering the holy places of Yahweh’s house. Yahweh calls it “the vengeance of his temple” in 51:11, so the destruction described here is justice, not conquest.

## Translation Issues in This Chapter

### Shifting speakers

The speakers in this chapter vary between Yahweh, Jeremiah the prophet, the foreigners who had tried to heal Babylon in 51:9–10, and the people of Zion in 51:34–35, often with no introduction. Decide who is speaking in each section, and mark the changes in a way that your readers can follow, such as in the UST.

### Babylon spoken of as a woman

The Hebrew word for “city” is feminine, so Babylon is called “she” and “her” throughout the chapter and is also addressed directly as “you,” as a way to address the people who live there. If feminine forms or shifts between third person and second person would confuse your readers, you may use a phrase such as “the people of Babylon” or repeat the city’s name.

# Jeremiah 52 General Notes

## Structure and Formatting

The chapter returns to a previous sequence of events and describes how the Babylonians conquered Judah and destroyed the temple in Jerusalem.

Because of the statement “Jeremiah’s words end here” in Jeremiah 51:64, and because the text of this chapter also appears in 2 Kings 24:18–25:30, many scholars believe that someone other than Jeremiah wrote this chapter and attached to the scroll that Jeremiah and Baruch wrote.
